description.summary: The multi-headed hound of Greek mythology that guards the gates of Hades, preventing the dead from leaving. Most famously captured by Heracles as his twelfth and final labour.
description.full: Cerberus (Greek: Kérberos) is the monstrous hound that guards the gates of Hades in Greek and Roman mythology. He is the offspring of the giants Typhon and Echidna, and the brother of the Lernaean Hydra, the Chimera, and the two-headed dog Orthrus. Ancient sources differ on his appearance: Hesiod's Theogony assigns him fifty heads and a 'voice of bronze', and Pindar one hundred heads, while the dominant tradition from the late Archaic period onward gives him three heads, often with a serpent for a tail and snakes growing from his body. His role is to keep the dead within the underworld; the Greeks believed the dead could enter Hades freely but could not leave, and Cerberus enforces that one-way passage. The most famous story involving him is Heracles' Twelfth Labour, in which the hero descends into Hades, wrestles Cerberus into submission with his bare hands (using only his lion-skin as armour) and brings him up to King Eurystheus before returning him. Cerberus also appears in the catabases of Orpheus (charmed asleep by music) and Aeneas (in Virgil's Aeneid VI, drugged with a honey-and-herb cake by the Sibyl). He is a prolific subject of Greek vase-painting and Roman sculpture and survives in modern usage in the names of the Kerberos network authentication protocol and a genus of fanged snakes.

etymology.origin: Ancient Greek Kérberos (Κέρβερος); a long-standing but disputed Indo-European derivation links it to a root meaning 'spotted'.
etymology.meaning: Possibly 'spotted' (cf. Sanskrit śárvara-); the etymology remains debated.
etymology.first_use: Earliest substantial Greek attestations are Hesiodic (c. 700 BCE).

related_phenomena.name: Orthrus
related_phenomena.description: Cerberus's two-headed brother, dog of Geryon, also offspring of Typhon and Echidna

related_phenomena.name: Garmr
related_phenomena.description: Norse hound of Hel; comparable underworld hound

related_phenomena.name: Hellhound (general)
related_phenomena.description: Generic 'hound of hell' figure in later European folklore

coloration: black (most common in art and literature)

features.description: Three in the dominant tradition; fifty in Hesiod; one hundred in Pindar
A serpent or dragon-tail in place of a normal canine tail
Hesiodic and later sources describe snakes sprouting from the back, mane, or shoulders
Hesiod gives Cerberus a 'voice of bronze' — a terrible, resonant bark
Build of an enormous mastiff-type dog

physical.morphology: Canid base body modified by polycephaly and serpentine elements; consistently chthonic in colouring.

abilities.description: Permits the dead to enter but prevents them from leaving
Charmed asleep by Orpheus's lyre; sedated by the Sibyl's drugged cake in the Aeneid
Hesiod and later authors emphasise his terrifying voice

habitat_preference: the entrance to the Greek underworld (the gates of Hades)
the banks of the Styx and Acheron
behavior.diet: Implied carnivore; in tradition food and drugged cakes are the standard means of pacifying him.
patterns: Stationed at the gates of Hades
Allows the dead to enter but not to leave
Subdued only by exceptional heroes (Heracles) or by music/magic (Orpheus, Aeneas via the Sibyl)

range.description: In classical mythology Cerberus is located at the entrance to the Greek underworld; the entrance was traditionally placed at sites such as Cape Tainaron in Laconia and Lake Avernus in Campania.

hotspots.name: Cape Tainaron

location.description: Southern tip of the Mani peninsula; mythological entrance to Hades from which Heracles is said to have brought Cerberus up

hotspots.notes: Traditional Greek entrance to the underworld.

peak_activity_periods.description: Continuous classical literary and artistic tradition

origins.cultural_roots: Archaic Greek mythology; an underworld guardian within the chthonic family of monsters descending from Typhon and Echidna.
origins.earliest_accounts: Hesiod's Theogony (c. 700 BCE) and Homeric references.
origins.folklore_connections: Comparable to Norse Garmr, Egyptian Anubis (as psychopomp), and the Hindu hounds of Yama (the Sarameyas).

timeline.event: Hesiod's Theogony names Cerberus as offspring of Typhon and Echidna with fifty heads and a voice of bronze
Pindar describes Cerberus with one hundred heads (5th c. BCE)
timeline.significance: Pindar's number is the maximum recorded

timeline.event: Virgil's Aeneid VI depicts Aeneas's descent past Cerberus, who is sedated with a honey-and-herb cake by the Sibyl (c. 19 BCE)
Ovid retells the Heracles–Cerberus story in Metamorphoses VII
timeline.significance: Standard Latin literary version of the Twelfth Labour

timeline.event: Apollodorus's Bibliotheca (2nd c. CE) gives the standard prose narrative of Heracles wrestling Cerberus into submission

history.modern_era: Cerberus remains a continuous presence in Western culture, featuring in Dante's Inferno, modern fantasy literature and games, and lending his name to the Kerberos network authentication protocol developed at MIT in 1988.

documentary.name: Caeretan hydria with Heracles and Cerberus (c. 530 BCE)
documentary.description: Late-6th-century BCE black-figure hydria from Caere depicting Heracles leading Cerberus before Eurystheus, an early canonical artistic record.
documentary.analysis: One of the most-cited early visual records of the Twelfth Labour.

scientific.name: Indo-European underworld-hound motif
scientific.description: Comparative-mythology hypothesis that Cerberus belongs to a Proto-Indo-European inheritance of underworld-guarding hounds shared with the Norse Garmr and the Vedic hounds of Yama.
evidence_cited: Cognate roles of Garmr and the Sarameyas

skeptical.name: Documented mythological figure
skeptical.description: Cerberus is recorded as a mythological and artistic figure of Greek and Roman tradition. There is no zoological or paranormal claim attached to him in mainstream scholarship.
evidence_cited: Continuous textual and artistic tradition; absence of any cryptozoological claim

stories: Heracles' Twelfth Labour: capture of Cerberus
Orpheus charms Cerberus to sleep with his lyre
The Sibyl drugs Cerberus with a honey-and-herb cake (Virgil, Aeneid VI)
folklore.beliefs: In antiquity Cerberus was understood as a guardian of the threshold between life and death; he is not typically the object of cult but is invoked as an emblem of the inescapability of death.

literature: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone — J. K. Rowling (1997, as 'Fluffy')
film_tv: Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief (2010)

researchers.name: Walter Burkert
researchers.contribution: Studies of Greek mythology and chthonic ritual

researchers.name: Bruce Lincoln
researchers.contribution: Comparative Indo-European mythology including underworld-hound motifs

organizations.name: Society for the Promotion of Hellenic Studies
organizations.focus: Scholarly study of ancient Greek culture and mythology

research.ongoing_studies: Cerberus appears regularly in Classical Studies and comparative-mythology scholarship; not the subject of cryptozoological investigation.
